faq.q: Why does ethanol protect in methanol poisoning?

faq.q: Can haemodialysis be done without a dialysis machine?

faq.a: Delayed visual disturbances together with a high‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis after ingestion of homemade alcohol.
faq.q: What is the key bedside clue?

exam: A patient presents 18 h after drinking a local brew with blurred vision and metabolic acidosis. What is your next step? — Check ABG, start IV ethanol or fomepizole, and arrange dialysis if pH < 7.25.
How does formic acid cause blindness? — It inhibits cytochrome c oxidase in retinal mitochondria, leading to cellular hypoxia and optic nerve edema.
Why is fomepizole preferred over ethanol in most settings? — It specifically inhibits ADH without causing CNS depression or hypoglycaemia.
What laboratory finding distinguishes methanol from ethylene glycol poisoning? — Absence of calcium oxalate crystals in urine and presence of visual symptoms point to methanol.
In a facility without methanol assay, which clinical features confirm the diagnosis? — History of illicit alcohol, delayed visual loss, high‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis.
When is haemodialysis indicated even if fomepizole is started? — pH < 7.25, visual loss, or methanol level > 50 mg/dL despite ADH inhibition.
What are the risks of using high‑dose ethanol in a child? — Hypoglycaemia, respiratory depression, and difficulty titrating therapeutic levels.
How would you manage a pregnant woman with methanol poisoning? — Use fomepizole (category B), avoid high‑dose ethanol, correct acidosis, and consider dialysis; monitor fetal well‑being.
ai.title: Methanol Metabolism and Toxicity
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Methanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde, then to formic acid, causing metabolic acidosis and optic nerve damage. Understanding this pathway guides diagnosis and emergency management, especially where labs are limited.

b: Source: contaminated spirits, industrial exposure, accidental ingestion
Key toxic metabolite: formic acid
Typical latency: 12–24 h after ingestion
sections.p: Methanol, a common industrial solvent and contaminant in illicit spirits, is harmless until metabolised. The liver enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) converts it to formaldehyde, which is rapidly turned into formic acid by aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH). Formic acid accumulates, leading to high anion‑gap metabolic acidosis and ocular toxicity.

b: ADH: NAD⁺‑dependent, also metabolises ethanol
ALDH: rapid conversion, but capacity limited
Formic acid: primary cause of acidosis and visual loss
sections.p: ADH oxidises methanol (CH₃OH) to formaldehyde (CH₂O). ALDH then oxidises formaldehyde to formic acid (HCOOH). Formic acid inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase, impairing oxidative phosphorylation and causing cellular hypoxia, especially in the retina and basal ganglia.

b: Ethanol: 0.1–0.2 g/kg IV bolus then infusion
sections.p: Ethanol competitively inhibits ADH, slowing methanol conversion and buying time for treatment. Fomepizole, a synthetic ADH inhibitor, is the preferred antidote where available.

b: Acidosis: pH < 7.35, HCO₃⁻ < 20 mmol/L
Visual symptoms: decreased acuity, scotomas, painful eye movements
Neurologic: headache, seizures, coma
sections.p: Excess formic acid overwhelms buffering systems, producing a high‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis (AG > 12 mmol/L). Accumulation in the optic nerve leads to blurred vision, “snowfield” visual loss, and possible permanent blindness.

b: History of homemade alcohol or industrial exposure
Delayed onset of symptoms (12‑48 h)
Rapid deterioration without treatment
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, methanol poisoning often follows consumption of illicit brews. Early recognition relies on history, visual changes, and a high‑anion‑gap acidosis. Lack of fomepizole means ethanol therapy and haemodialysis become critical.

t.b: Is there a high‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis? – pH < 7.35, AG > 12 mmol/L confirms metabolic disturbance.
Is methanol present at toxic levels? – > 20 mg/dL suggests toxicity; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture.
Is formic acid elevated? – Direct marker of toxicity; not essential if other data fit.
Are there optic disc changes or retinal hemorrhages? – Supports ocular toxicity.

t.a: Urine or breath analysis for methanol (portable kits)
t.b: Is methanol detectable? – Useful where lab assays are absent.

b: Ethanol infusion (if fomepizole unavailable) – competitive ADH inhibition
Fomepizole – preferred ADH inhibitor, less respiratory depression
Sodium bicarbonate IV – raise pH, improve formate clearance
Haemodialysis – rapid removal of methanol and formate, corrects acidosis; indicated if pH < 7.25, visual loss, or methanol > 50 mg/dL
Supportive care: airway protection, seizure control, monitor electrolytes
sections.p: Stop further absorption, inhibit ADH, correct acidosis, and remove formic acid.

b: Ethanol: causes low‑anion‑gap acidosis, no visual loss, rapid recovery
Ethylene glycol: produces calcium oxalate crystals, renal failure, no prominent visual symptoms
sections.p: Ethanol intoxication and ethylene glycol poisoning.
